extracted.intended_audience: observational astronomers and experimental natural philosophers (17th-century readers; researchers reproducing observations/experiments)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting and reporting astronomical observations (planets, satellites, tides) and experimental natural philosophy (frigorific experiments), emphasizing instrumentation, repeated/distant observations, controls, and clear procedural detail. Suitable for authors submitting observational reports and experimental demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hasty conclusions from few observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Those astronomers were too hasty in determining, after five or six observations only, in how much time Mars finished his revolution; he denies it to be performed in 13 hours... though he himself had observed for a much longer time than they, yet he durst not for a great while define whether Mars made but one turn in 24 hours 40 minutes, or two; and that all that he could for a long time affirm, was only this, that after 24 h. 40 m. this planet appeared in the same manner he did before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not determine planetary rotation periods (or analogous periodic phenomena) from only a handful of observations; gather longer sequences of observations before asserting periods. Present provisional conclusions and reserve final determination until sufficient data are collected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple observations across dates to prove or refute periodicity
rubrics_metrics.description: He adduces numbered observations (e.g., saw first face Feb 6 at 11 o'clock and did not see it after 18 days at the same hour as he ought to have done if period were 12h.20m; analogously with Feb 24, March 27 etc.) to infer the true period ~24h.40m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit dated/time-stamped observations and show how they contradict alternative period hypotheses (give multiple instances spanning relevant intervals). Number and explain specific observational tests that would follow from a proposed period and show whether they are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare observations from distant observers/locations
rubrics_metrics.description: More exactly to be determined by comparing distant observations... Cassini pretends to evidence by his observations, made at the same time at Bononia, that the same day and hour those spots were very large...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corroborate local observations with those made at other places to resolve ambiguities (e.g., face-identification, apparent size/position) and to settle periods or geometrical interpretation differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish different planetary 'faces' / features carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who affirm the former must have been deceived by not well distinguishing the two faces, and by having seen the second, mistaking it for the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly identify and describe distinct faces or configurations (use labelled figures) to avoid confusing different appearances of a rotating body; mis-identification is an anti-pattern leading to wrong period estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid atmospheric/horizon effects that deceive early/low observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Because he might be imposed upon by vapours, whilst Mars was yet so near the horizon, he gives this other determination...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer observations made when the object is higher above the horizon; note atmospheric conditions and treat near-horizon sightings with caution. Use additional determinations when early/low observations could be biased by vapours or haze.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report precise dates, times, durations and sequence of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: I observed the body of Jupiter ... June 26th, between three and four o'clock in the morning ... I saw the limb pretty round ... I perceived, about 3h.15m. near the middle ... observed it in about 10 minutes time to be got almost to d ... at 3h.25m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record exact calendar dates, clock times (to minutes if possible), durations and intermediate times to allow others to reproduce timing-based inferences (motions, eclipses, transits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify instrumentation and measurement details
rubrics_metrics.description: I observed ... through a 60 foot-glass ... found the apparent diameter ... through the tube ... a sealed thermoscope (containing tinctured spirit of wine) was 16 inches long, the ball [bulb] about the size of a walnut, and the diameter of the tube about an 8th or 10th of an inch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State instrument type and key dimensions (telescope focal length/‘foot’ length, thermoscope length, bulb size, tube diameter). These details are essential for assessing observational resolution and experimental sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include labelled figures and descriptive morphological labelling
rubrics_metrics.description: as is represented by the fig. O ... which is that of the second face of Mars ... (fig. Q. pi. 2) ... the one of which (h) was a small dark belt crossing the body southward...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use figures with labels for faces, belts, spots, limbs, rings, etc., and reference them in the text to make morphological descriptions unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and interpret satellite positions and shadows
rubrics_metrics.description: I perceived ... a very dark round spot ... which was nothing else save the shadow of the satellite h, eclipsing a part of the face of Jupiter. ... the other three satellites ... were westwards of the body of Jupiter; appearing as bright through the tube as the body of Jupiter did to the naked eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track satellites' relative positions and note eclipse events; distinguish surface markings from satellite shadows; state how satellites move relative to disk features to aid interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record atmospheric conditions and use auxiliary instruments (baroscope)
rubrics_metrics.description: After which, the air growing very hazy, and as appeared by the baroscope very light also in weight, I could not observe it;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note atmospheric transparency/seeing and use available instruments (baroscope, thermometer) to document reasons for loss of visibility; report when observations are aborted for atmospheric reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe experimental protocol with quantities, materials and steps (frigorific mixture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take 1 lb. of powdered sal ammoniac and about three pints or pounds of water; put the salt into the liquor, either altogether, if your design be to produce an intense but short coldness; or, at two, three, or four several times, if you desire that the produced coldness should rather last somewhat longer than be so great. Stir the powder in the liquor with a stick or whalebone (or some other thing that will not be acted upon by the brine) to hasten the dissolution of the salt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give exact ingredient masses/volumes, recommend inert stirring implements, and describe variations in addition method according to desired intensity/duration. Provide step-by-step modes for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide multiple, independent tests to demonstrate effect (how to evince cold)
rubrics_metrics.description: That a considerable degree of cold is really produced by this is evident, 1st. To the touch; 2dly, By the dew which collects on the sides of the vessel containing the solution; 3dly, By plunging into it a good sealed weather-glass furnished with tinctured spirit of wine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use several lines of evidence (subjective touch, condensation, and quantitative thermoscope/thermometer measurements) to establish the effect; favour the sealed thermoscope/thermometer as the surest test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerate factors affecting intensity and duration and how to control them
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration of the cold produced by this experiment depends upon several circumstances; as, 1st, Upon the season of the year and present temperature of the air; 2dly, Upon the quantity of the salt and water; 3dly, Upon the goodness and fitness of the particular parcel of salt that is employed; 4thly, Upon the way of putting the salt into the water; ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List environmental and procedural variables (season/ambient temperature, reagent purity, masses, manner and rate of addition, particle size, stirring) and explain how changing each variable will affect outcome. Suggest ways to prolong or intensify the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advise practical techniques for applying experimental results (cooling drinks, freezing water)
rubrics_metrics.description: To cool drinks with this mixture, you may put them in thin glasses, the thinner the better; which (their orifices being stopped and kept above the mixture) may be moved to and fro in it, the liquor being then immediately poured out and drank. ... water thinly placed on the outside of the glass, whilst the mixture was quickly stirred up and down, would freeze in a quarter of a minute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete procedural advice for applied uses (how to cool glasses, how to freeze water quickly) including vessel choices and motions to maximize heat transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: State limitations, untested claims and invite further trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether sal ammoniac mixed with sand or earth, and not dissolved, but only moistened with a little water sprinkled upon it, will answer for cooling bottles of wine or other liquors, Mr. Boyle says he did not satisfy himself by a sufficient number of trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly say what has not been sufficiently tried and avoid making conclusive claims where replication/trials are lacking. Encourage further testing to settle open questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe methods for reagent recovery / economy
rubrics_metrics.description: The sal ammoniac employed in these experiments may be recovered (to save expense) by evaporating the solution, and crystallizing it. The salt thus obtained will serve again for fresh frigorific mixtures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include post-experiment procedures for reclaiming reagents/materials (evaporation and recrystallization) when relevant to economy or sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare new hypotheses to existing theories and treat proposals as essays to be tested
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not profess to be so well skilled in the history of tides, as to undertake presently to accommodate my general hypothesis to particular cases; or indeed to undertake for the certainty of it, but only as an essay propose it to further consideration, to stand or fall, as it shall be found to answer matter of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing theoretical explanations, acknowledge limits of current evidence, compare with prior accounts (Galileo, others), and present the hypothesis as a testable essay rather than asserted truth; seek further empirical history/data to fit particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mechanical analogies and compound-motion reasoning to explain fluid phenomena (tides)
rubrics_metrics.description: An acceleration or retardation of the vessel which carries it, will cause a rising of the water in one part, and a falling in another; ... the true motion of each part of the earth's surface being compounded of those two motions, the annual and diurnal ... which would afford us a cause of two tides in twenty-four hours; the one upon the greatest acceleration of motion, the other upon its greatest retardation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ clear mechanical examples/analogies (moving vessel, compound motions) to build intuitive explanations for observed fluid behaviour; decompose motions (diurnal + annual) to obtain testable consequences (e.g., two tides/day) and then account for observed deviations (monthly shift).
